summary: Defines a textual representation for Autonomous System numbers as the plain decimal value, to be used by all documents, systems and user interfaces. This is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Every network has a number. This memo says everyone should write that number the ordinary way, as a plain decimal like 65000, so nobody gets confused.

questions: how to write an as number
asplain format for autonomous system numbers
subtitle: Use decimal notation for all Autonomous System numbers.

tldr.problem: Autonomous System numbers could be represented in three different formats—asplain (decimal), asdot (mixed notation for compatibility), and asdot+ (high.low pairs)—causing confusion in documentation, configuration systems, and tools.
tldr.mechanism: Standardize on asplain, which represents every AS number as a single decimal integer without field delimiters, matching the internal structure-less way AS numbers are used in inter-domain routing.
tldr.outcome: A single consistent notation throughout all documentation, systems, and user interfaces eliminates ambiguity and simplifies AS number handling.

today: RFC 5396 is a Proposed Standard. Asplain representation is now the standard in IANA registries and virtually all modern routing systems and documentation.

sections.title: Why one format matters
sections.content: Autonomous System numbers identify networks in inter-domain routing. For many years, the IANA and routing system have treated AS numbers as unstructured 32-bit integers. However, because 32-bit addresses felt limited before extended addressing, people began using a two-part notation similar to IP addresses. This led to multiple representation formats being used simultaneously in different systems, causing confusion when the same AS number might appear as 65526 in one system and 0.65526 in another.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine if phone numbers could be written as 5551234567 or 555-123-4567 or 555-1234, all meaning the same thing. Everyone would get confused. One format is clearer.

sections.title: The three formats
sections.content: The asplain format represents all AS numbers using simple decimal notation, like 65546. The asdot+ format represents AS numbers using two 16-bit parts joined by a period, like 1.10, for use when the number exceeds 16-bit capacity. The asdot format used asplain for numbers less than 65536 but asdot+ for larger numbers. Only asplain avoids this inconsistency.
sections.plainLanguage: The three ways were: all-decimal (asplain), big-number-small-number (asdot+), or mix them (asdot). Asplain is simplest.

sections.title: The standard: asplain
sections.content: RFC 5396 designates asplain as the single textual representation for AS numbers in all documentation, configuration systems, reports, and tools. The asplain representation directly corresponds to the AS number's internal use in routing without any artificial structure. IANA registries must use decimal representation for AS numbers, making asplain the official standard.
sections.plainLanguage: From now on, write every AS number as plain decimals. That's the rule everyone agreed on.
